## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\vspace{1em}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}

_What physical failure modes remain invisible to modern runtime detectors, and how must an engineer govern what evidence cannot settle?_

An engineering record can depend on a physical condition the machine cannot observe. A stopping claim may assume sufficient friction, while the available sensors cannot establish that assumption before every maneuver. Successful trials do not supply the missing measurement or show machine behavior outside tested conditions. Such gaps require an explicit account of what remains unsupported and how that uncertainty limits operation. A runtime detector can support a safety argument only for failures it can reveal in time for an effective response. Where that evidence is unavailable, engineers must evaluate whether reduced speed or restricted access provides adequate containment, or whether operation should be withheld. These limits belong in the architecture and release decision. The physical AI stack remains accountable only when claims about the brain, nervous system, and body stay within the reach of the evidence supporting them.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↰ **Prerequisite:** The four foundational physical laws synthesize the opening principles from @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws.
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Assess which safety claims exceed the evidence available for a specific physical machine
- Evaluate whether a detector can identify a hazard before effective intervention becomes impossible
- Define operational restrictions and closure tests for unsupported claims in the engineering record
- Apply physical budgets, information age, authority separation, and evidence requirements to an unfamiliar machine

:::

## Epistemic Limits {#sec-frontier-epistemic-limits}

Consider a transport robot whose stopping calculation assumes tire friction $\mu\ge0.60$. An unmonitored oil patch lowers friction to $\mu=0.15$; under the same speed and response delay, the friction-limited braking term becomes four times larger. The controller can meet its timing deadline and still overrun the reserved clearance. The missing evidence is the local friction floor before braking begins. Which physical premises can the machine establish in time, and what operation remains justified when it cannot?

::: {#dfn-frontier-embodied-latency-scaling-law .callout-definition title="Embodied latency scaling law"}

***Embodied latency scaling law***\index{Embodied latency scaling law!definition}\index{Scaling laws!embodied latency} is the physical constraint dictating that scaling neural policy parameter count yields diminishing operational safety returns unless inference latency decreases proportionally, because physical reaction distance $d_{\text{react}} = v \cdot (t_{\text{inference}} + t_{\text{actuation}}) + \frac{v^2}{2 a_{\max}}$ scales linearly with computational delay.

1.  **Significance**: Establishes that intelligence in physical systems cannot be scaled purely by adding model parameters, because computational delay directly degrades dynamic stability and spatial stopping clearance.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike compute scaling laws in static language modeling where latency affects only token generation speed, embodied latency scaling directly couples computational delay to mechanical reaction time constants ($t_{\text{react}} \ge t_{\text{inference}} + t_{\text{actuation}}$).
3.  **Common pitfall**: Deploying multi-billion parameter foundation models directly in the closed-loop control path under the assumption that greater semantic reasoning compensates for an unbudgeted response delay.

:::

As the final chapter of this book, Frontier Limits represents the capstone of Tier 4 (System Governance & Assurance) and the outer boundary of the four-tier architecture stack in @fig-17-locator. Throughout this text, we have architected an end-to-end discipline designed to take physical AI from experimental prototypes to dependable machines:

- **The Body (Tier 1):** governing continuous plant dynamics, actuator torque/speed curves, friction limits, and thermal dissipation;[^fn-bridge-frontier-body]
- **The Nervous System (Tier 2):** providing deterministic real-time communication, microsecond scheduling, hardware isolation, and barrier-certificate enforcement;[^fn-bridge-frontier-nervous]
- **The Brain (Tier 3):** generating learned representations, multimodal perception, and long-horizon deliberative planning;[^fn-bridge-frontier-brain] and
- **System Governance & Assurance (Tier 4):** orchestrating shared authority, whole-system verification, and auditable release safety cases.[^fn-bridge-frontier-governance]

[^fn-bridge-frontier-body]: **Continuous Plant Dynamics and Mechanical Margins**\index{Plant dynamics!Tier 1 frontier}: As established in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary and @sec-body-five-budgets, the physical plant imposes hard thermodynamic and kinematic limits. When software detectors fail, mechanical dissipation, passive compliance, and structural margins are candidate protections whose limits still need evidence. Operating without these physical margins risks uncontained kinetic impacts during sensor blind spots.

[^fn-bridge-frontier-nervous]: **Microsecond Determinism and Real-Time Seams**\index{Deterministic fieldbuses!Tier 2 frontier}: As detailed in @sec-nervous-multi-rate-bridge and @sec-placement-silicon-substrate, Tier 2 bridges the asynchronous world of neural inference to the hard real-time demands of actuation. Its watchdogs and fieldbus arbitration support timing only within measured response and interference bounds. Loss of observability requires a separately validated state-dependent fallback while sufficient clearance remains.

[^fn-bridge-frontier-brain]: **Deliberative Reasoning and Proposal Boundaries**\index{Cognitive proposal boundary!Tier 3 frontier}: As developed in @sec-brain-embodied and @sec-planning-kinodynamic-feasibility, Tier 3 models propose complex behaviors in continuous state spaces. Their performance may improve with compute, while admitted motion remains contingent on external verification and enforcement. Allowing unverified neural trajectories to bypass deterministic enforcement risks driving actuators into kinematic singularities or destructive collisions.

[^fn-bridge-frontier-governance]: **Assurance Frameworks and Governance Seams**\index{Governance synthesis!Tier 4 frontier}: As structured in @sec-intervention-shared-authority, @sec-verification-fault-injection, and @sec-release-decision-to-deploy, Tier 4 binds authority arbitration, qualification ladders, and goal-structured safety cases into an accountable engineering discipline. This governance tier ensures that empirical verification records and residual assumptions remain auditable across continuous model retrains. Without structured lifecycle governance, silent distribution shift can erode safety margins without triggering telemetry alarms.

Yet every engineering method has a boundary where its guarantees expire. As captured by the Embodied Latency Scaling Law in \ref{dfn-frontier-embodied-latency-scaling-law}, simply scaling the parameter count of foundation models cannot circumvent physical mechanics: computational delay directly consumes the physical reaction time constant of the plant. Furthermore, as governed by Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety [@ashby1956introduction], a controller cannot regulate disturbances that its sensory architecture cannot perceive. Consider three canonical machines whose line items close perfectly on paper:

1. **A mobile transport platform:** moving at $1.5\text{ m/s}$, whose stopping claim of $0.49\text{ m}$ assumes tire friction $\mu \ge 0.60$. When unmonitored surface liquid drops friction to $\mu = 0.15$, braking distance quadruples from $0.19\text{ m}$ to $0.76\text{ m}$, expanding total stopping distance to $1.06\text{ m}$ and breaching the $0.80\text{ m}$ clearance buffer;
2. **An articulated manipulator:** commanded to limit contact force to $40\text{ N}$, where the guarantee assumes structural stiffness across its end-effector mount. When fatigue micro-cracking introduces unmodeled mechanical compliance, the mount stores strain energy under load and releases it abruptly during surface transitions, delivering an unmeasured $120\text{ N}$ transient peak while joint torque sensors register nominal values; and
3. **A chemical flow regulator:** maintaining line pressure below $200\text{ kPa}$, whose control loop assumes an undrifted diaphragm pressure transducer. When chemical deposition induces a steady calibration drift of $0.5\text{ kPa/h}$, the nervous system throttles against a phantom pressure spike or opens into an actual overpressure state of $240\text{ kPa}$, unaware that its reference sensor has drifted from physical ground truth.

In each constructed case, the machine can leave the assumed envelope while its available telemetry remains nominal. A one-sided 95 percent zero-event bound at $10^{-9}\text{ h}^{-1}$ under a stationary Poisson model needs about three billion failure-free hours. This **astronomical exposure wall** makes fleet testing alone inadequate for such a release cadence; it does not make the hours mathematically impossible to accumulate. The safety case must name the missing premise, restrict operation while it remains open, and state what evidence could close it.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↰ **Prerequisite:** The statistical impossibility of exhaustive testing expands upon the Butler & Finelli limits in @sec-evaluation-trial-limits.
:::

The chapter tests that discipline against finite exposure, unobservable friction and material states, and an unfamiliar packaging cell. Each example asks what the machine can measure, what its actuators can still prevent, and which claim must remain open.

::: {#chk-frontier-epistemic-horizons-and-unobservable-states .callout-checkpoint title="Epistemic horizons and unobservable physical dynamics"}

Before asserting safety claims over high-capacity neural policies in open physical environments, verify your understanding of fundamental epistemic limits:

- [ ] **Observationally indistinguishable world states**: Can you identify failure modes where benign and catastrophic physical conditions produce mathematically identical sensor telemetry ($y_A(t) \equiv y_B(t)$) up to the system's action deadline?
- [ ] **Scale-invariant epistemic blind spots**: Can you explain why increasing neural network parameter counts, dataset size, or inference compute cannot resolve latent physical states that emit zero observable physical energy prior to harm?
- [ ] **Latent shortcut learning**: Can you describe how deep perception models exploit non-causal visual features as proxies for unmeasured physical properties, commanding destructive actions with near-zero softmax entropy?
- [ ] **Proposal-permission architectural containment**: Can you explain why unmodeled physical risks demand structural, out-of-band permission barriers rather than relying on internal policy uncertainty or self-assessment?

*Confusing high statistical confidence with physical truth is the quintessential failure mode of physical AI. Ensure all safety-critical invariants are anchored in observable physical mechanics rather than latent policy representations.*
:::

## What the Method Cannot Establish {#sec-frontier-method-limits}

A safety release claim for a physical AI system is not a monolithic assertion. Its necessary links depend on the hazards and protection chosen. The argument must establish the operating domain, measured actuator and stopping bounds, component contracts, and independent permission for learned proposals (@sec-brain-embodied). Hazards controlled by runtime detection also need measured detector coverage and timely monitoring. Hazards controlled by passive limits or operating restrictions instead need evidence that those measures hold over the declared load, wear, and exposure envelope. Generating extensive evidence for one link cannot compensate for an unsupported premise in another.[^fn-hist-popper-falsification]

[^fn-hist-popper-falsification]: **Popperian Falsification**\index{Falsification!Popperian induction}: Karl Popper formalized the asymmetry of empirical induction: no finite sequence of safe observations can prove universal safety, whereas a single counterexample refutes it. Operational fleet hours establish survival rates strictly under observed stationary conditions, not out-of-distribution guarantees. Extrapolating zero observed incidents to unbounded environments produces an illusory sense of safety that fails upon encountering unmodeled edge cases.

Every link in a safety case requires an explicit **epistemic classification**\index{Epistemic classification}, identifying each premise as measured directly through physical instrumentation, derived analytically from measured premises, assumed on physical or operational grounds, decided by accountable judgment, left unsupported by existing data, or explicitly declared outside the threat model. In the three reference machines examined throughout this text, these classifications reveal the exact boundary where evidence ends. For the wheeled mobile robot, the stopping-distance guarantee relies on an assumed friction coefficient between tire and floor that cannot be measured before braking begins. For the articulated manipulator, the collision-containment argument depends on an assumed material-damage threshold for surrounding equipment, which is an engineering judgment about structural yield rather than a measured property of the controller. For the aerial vehicle, the state-estimation envelope assumes statistical independence between optical flow and inertial sensors, an assumption that collapses under sudden illumination changes or frame resonance. Naming these premises explicitly does not weaken the release record. It establishes the physical envelope within which the release verdict is justified, and outside of which the verdict ceases to apply.

Separating measurement from judgment is fundamental to systems engineering discipline. Empirical testing and statistical characterization can estimate physical exposure, quantify sensor noise, and bound parametric uncertainty, but no measurement can choose an acceptable **residual risk**\index{Residual risk} or decide which individuals in an operational environment must bear that risk. Those choices are accountable human decisions that must be recorded as explicit judgments rather than disguised as empirical findings. In the same way, the **threat model**\index{Threat model} establishes an absolute boundary on the validity of the record. Empirical testing across nominal fleet operations and accidental component faults provides no evidence regarding intentional adversarial attacks. A safety record demonstrating that a vision pipeline handles sensor noise, lens blur, and partial occlusions provides zero statistical support for claims about resilience against adversarial optical projection, model parameter tampering, or intentional denial of service across the internal communication bus.

```{python}
#| label: calc-frontier-architectural-shield-dilution
#| echo: false
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_sci, fmt_int, fmt, fmt_multiple, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_empirical_testing_exposure,
    calc_shielded_system_hazard_rate,
)

# ┌── 1. INPUT (Illustrative target and distinct evidence records) ────
p_target = 1.0e-9  # assumed system incidents/hour target, not a statutory rate
confidence = 0.95
alpha = 1.0 - confidence

fleet_units = 100
t_cycle_days = 90.0
hours_per_day = 24.0
hours_per_year = 8766  # total hours in a year

c_shield_assumed = 0.9999  # class-specific interception coverage needs separate evidence
p_hw_assumed = 0.0  # illustration only; hardware and common-cause risk need evidence
proposal_events_hypothetical = 0  # separate counterfactual-oracle proposal log
proposal_exposure_hours_hypothetical = 216000.0

# ┌── 2. COMPUTE (Astronomical exposure vs shield decomposition) ───────
n_astronomical_hours = calc_empirical_testing_exposure(p_target, confidence=confidence)
machine_years_astronomical = n_astronomical_hours.magnitude / hours_per_year
fleet_calendar_years = machine_years_astronomical / fleet_units

# Quarterly cycle exposure: zero observed system events bound the integrated system rate.
t_cycle_hours = t_cycle_days * hours_per_day
n_cycle_hours = fleet_units * t_cycle_hours
p_system_observed_upper = -math.log(alpha) / n_cycle_hours
ratio_empirical_to_target = p_system_observed_upper / p_target

# Conditional design arithmetic: a separately observed hazardous-proposal rate
# and class-specific interception coverage would be required to use this model.
p_proposal_limit = (p_target - p_hw_assumed) / (1.0 - c_shield_assumed)
n_brain_hours = calc_empirical_testing_exposure(p_proposal_limit, confidence=confidence)
t_test_days = n_brain_hours.magnitude / (fleet_units * hours_per_day)
t_test_months = t_test_days / (365.25 / 12.0)
p_proposal_upper_hypothetical = -math.log(alpha) / proposal_exposure_hours_hypothetical
p_system_conditional = calc_shielded_system_hazard_rate(
    p_proposal_upper_hypothetical / ureg.hour, c_shield_assumed, p_hw_assumed / ureg.hour
).magnitude
c_required_cycle = 1.0 - (p_target - p_hw_assumed) / p_proposal_upper_hypothetical
test_overrun_days = t_test_days - t_cycle_days

# ┌── 3. GUARDS (Statistical bounds & invariance checks) ──────────────
check(abs(n_astronomical_hours.magnitude - 2.9957e9) < 1e7, f"Unexpected astronomical exposure: {n_astronomical_hours}")
check(abs(machine_years_astronomical - 341744.0) < 500.0, f"Unexpected machine years: {machine_years_astronomical}")
check(abs(fleet_calendar_years - 3417.4) < 10.0, f"Unexpected fleet calendar years: {fleet_calendar_years}")
check(abs(n_cycle_hours - 216000.0) < 1.0, f"Unexpected cycle hours: {n_cycle_hours}")
check(abs(p_system_observed_upper - 1.3869e-5) < 1e-8, f"Unexpected system rate: {p_system_observed_upper}")
check(abs(ratio_empirical_to_target - 13869.0) < 10.0, f"Unexpected ratio: {ratio_empirical_to_target}")
check(proposal_events_hypothetical == 0, "Proposal scenario requires zero events")
check(abs(p_proposal_limit - 1.0e-5) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected proposal limit: {p_proposal_limit}")
check(abs(n_brain_hours.magnitude - 299573.0) < 100.0, f"Unexpected brain exposure: {n_brain_hours}")
check(abs(t_test_days - 124.8) < 1.0, f"Unexpected test days: {t_test_days}")
check(abs(t_test_months - 4.1) < 0.1, f"Unexpected test months: {t_test_months}")
check(abs(p_system_conditional - 1.386913e-9) < 1e-12, f"Unexpected conditional residual: {p_system_conditional}")
check(abs(c_required_cycle - 0.9999278974) < 1e-8, f"Unexpected required coverage: {c_required_cycle}")
check(test_overrun_days > 34.0, f"Unexpected 90-day overrun: {test_overrun_days}")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Canonical formatting) ────────────────────────────────
class ArchitecturalShieldDilution:
    p_target_sci_str = fmt_sci(p_target)
    n_astronomical_sci_str = fmt_sci(n_astronomical_hours.magnitude)
    n_astronomical_sci_1dec_str = fmt_sci(n_astronomical_hours.magnitude, precision=1)
    machine_years_str = fmt_int(round(machine_years_astronomical), commas=True)
    machine_years_k_str = fmt_int(round(machine_years_astronomical / 1000.0) * 1000, commas=True)
    fleet_calendar_years_str = fmt_int(round(fleet_calendar_years))

    n_cycle_sci_str = fmt_sci(n_cycle_hours, precision=2)
    p_emp_sci_str = fmt_sci(p_system_observed_upper, precision=3)
    p_emp_sci_2dec_str = fmt_sci(p_system_observed_upper, precision=2)
    emp_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(ratio_empirical_to_target), precision=0, commas=True)
    emp_ratio_approx_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(ratio_empirical_to_target / 10.0) * 10, precision=0, commas=True)

    c_shield_str = fmt(c_shield_assumed, precision=4)
    p_brain_sci_str = fmt_sci(p_proposal_limit, precision=0)
    n_brain_sci_str = fmt_sci(n_brain_hours.magnitude, precision=2)
    t_test_days_str = fmt(t_test_days, precision=3)
    t_test_months_str = fmt(t_test_months, precision=1)
    p_system_conditional_sci_str = fmt_sci(p_system_conditional, precision=3)
    c_required_str = fmt(c_required_cycle, precision=7)
    test_overrun_days_str = fmt(test_overrun_days, precision=1)
```

Before counting hours, define the event, exposed population, operating conditions, rate target $\lambda$, confidence level $1-\alpha$, and dependence assumptions. For the illustrative $10^{-9}\text{ h}^{-1}$ target,[^fn-std-sil4-testing] a stationary homogeneous Poisson model gives $P(N(n)=0\mid\lambda)=e^{-\lambda n}$. With zero events, the one-sided upper rate is $\lambda_U=-\ln\alpha/n$; reaching $\lambda_U\le\lambda$ requires @eq-frontier-zero-failure-exposure:
$$n \ge \frac{-\ln \alpha}{p}$$ {#eq-frontier-zero-failure-exposure}
Evaluating @eq-frontier-zero-failure-exposure for $p = 10^{-9}\text{ failures/h}$ at 95 percent confidence ($\alpha = 0.05$) yields $n \ge -\ln(0.05) / 10^{-9} \approx$ `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.n_astronomical_sci_str` hours. Accumulating `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.n_astronomical_sci_1dec_str` operating hours without a single observed failure requires approximately `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.machine_years_str` machine-years of continuous execution ($1\text{ year} = 8{,}766\text{ h}$). For an operational fleet of $M = 100$ physical units running continuously, accumulating this empirical exposure requires $T_{\text{fleet}} \approx$ `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.fleet_calendar_years_str` calendar years (@fig-17-epistemic-limits, panel b). This threshold represents the **astronomical exposure wall**\index{Astronomical exposure wall!definition}: the mathematical scaling limit where a rare rate target requires exposure inversely proportional to that target, beyond this fleet’s proposed release interval (for the statistical derivation under Poisson and binomial models, see @sec-appendix-ml-exposure).[^fn-math-astronomical-wall] @Fig-17-exposure-scaling extends that relation across the full range of target rates, and the curve is the argument: because required exposure grows as the reciprocal of the probability being bounded, each additional order of magnitude of claimed safety costs an order of magnitude more operating time than the last.

[^fn-std-sil4-testing]: **Scope of the Rate**\index{IEC 61508!SIL 4 testing}: The $10^{-9}\text{ h}^{-1}$ rate is an illustrative system hazard target here. The IEC 61508 high-demand SIL 4 dangerous-failure band is $\ge10^{-9}$ to $<10^{-8}\text{ h}^{-1}$ in the [UK HSE functional-safety guide](https://www.hse.gov.uk/offshore/assets/docs/functional-safety-inspection-guide.pdf); it does not prescribe this chapter's target for every machine.

[^fn-math-astronomical-wall]: **Evidence Across Updates**\index{Astronomical exposure wall!retraining reset}: An updated model may alter the proposal distribution. Earlier data can be pooled only with a justified configuration-equivalence and exposure argument; an update does not automatically erase every observation. The Poisson model also requires a defensible treatment of shared fleet conditions and correlated faults.

::: {#fig-17-exposure-scaling fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Astronomical exposure wall**: Required failure-free exposure hours against target failure probability per hour, under a Poisson zero-event model at 95 percent confidence, with the equivalent machine-years on the opposing axis. Certifying $10^{-9}$ per hour demands roughly three billion failure-free hours, which this fleet cannot accumulate within its 90-day update interval." fig-alt="Log-log chart with an inverted horizontal axis showing required failure-free test hours rising as the target failure probability falls. A marked point at ten to the minus ninth per hour sits at roughly three billion hours, annotated as the astronomical exposure wall, with a second axis giving the equivalent machine-years."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz

data = pd.read_csv("vol4/17_frontier/data/exposure_scaling.csv")

fig, ax1, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(8, 5))

ax1.plot(data["target_failure_rate"], data["required_exposure_hours"], linewidth=2.5, color=COLORS["RedLine"])

ax1.set_xscale("log")
ax1.set_yscale("log")
ax1.invert_xaxis()

ax1.set_xlabel("Target Failure Probability ($p$) per hour", fontweight="bold")
ax1.set_ylabel("Required Failure-Free Hours ($n$)", color=COLORS["RedLine"], fontweight="bold")
ax1.tick_params(axis='y', labelcolor=COLORS["RedLine"])

# Annotate the astronomical limit
threshold_p = 1e-9
threshold_n = 2.9957 / threshold_p

ax1.axvline(x=threshold_p, color="black", linestyle="--", alpha=0.5)
ax1.axhline(y=threshold_n, color=COLORS["RedLine"], linestyle="--", alpha=0.5)
ax1.plot(threshold_p, threshold_n, marker="o", markersize=8, color=COLORS["RedLine"])

ax1.annotate(
    "Astronomical Exposure Wall\n$p = 10^{-9}$, $n \\approx 3 \\times 10^9$ h",
    xy=(threshold_p, threshold_n),
    xytext=(1e-7, 1e10),
    arrowprops=dict(facecolor='black', arrowstyle="->", alpha=0.7),
    fontsize=10,
    backgroundcolor="white",
)

ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax2.set_yscale("log")
ax2.set_ylim(ax1.get_ylim()[0] / (24 * 365.25), ax1.get_ylim()[1] / (24 * 365.25))
ax2.set_ylabel("Required Machine-Years", color=COLORS["primary"], fontweight="bold")
ax2.tick_params(axis='y', labelcolor=COLORS["primary"])

ax1.margins(x=0.14, y=0.14)
plt.tight_layout()

plt.show()
plt.close()
```

:::

::: {#nbk-frontier-fleet-exposure-and-shielded-decomposition .callout-notebook title="Fleet exposure and a conditional shield calculation"}

**Problem**: One hundred robots operate for 90 days with a shield. No catastrophic system event is observed. What does that exposure establish? Separately, suppose a counterfactual oracle could identify hazardous policy proposals, and a named shield's interception coverage were measured for that hazard class. Would an assumed coverage of 0.9999 suffice for an illustrative $10^{-9}\text{ h}^{-1}$ system target?

**Observed system record**: Under a stationary homogeneous Poisson model, $100\times90\times24=216{,}000$ fleet-hours and zero incidents give a one-sided 95 percent upper bound $\lambda_{\text{system},U}=-\ln(0.05)/216{,}000=$ `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_emp_sci_2dec_str` $\text{h}^{-1}$. This is `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.emp_ratio_approx_mult_str` above the illustrative target. Prevented hazardous proposals are absent from this incident count, so this result cannot be relabeled as a policy-proposal rate.

**Separate conditional design case**: Imagine a *different*, fully adjudicated proposal log with zero hazardous proposals in `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.n_cycle_sci_str` hours and a validated counterfactual hazard oracle. Its numerical upper bound is also `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_emp_sci_str` $\text{h}^{-1}$ only because its assumed exposure and count match. If class-specific shield interception coverage were independently established at $c=0.9999$, and hardware plus common-cause residual were assumed zero for this calculation, the modeled residual bound would be `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_system_conditional_sci_str` $\text{h}^{-1}$, **above** the target. The required coverage in that hypothetical is at least `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.c_required_str`; this is a design target, not measured coverage.

**Required proposal evidence at $c=0.9999$**: The proposal-rate bound must be at most $10^{-5}\text{ h}^{-1}$. Zero adjudicated hazardous proposals would require about $299{,}573$ independently modeled proposal-hours, or `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.t_test_days_str` days for 100 units, `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.test_overrun_days_str` days beyond this 90-day cycle. A policy update needs an explicit configuration-equivalence argument before older proposal evidence can be pooled; a changed policy does not automatically erase every earlier observation.

**Systems insight**: A shield changes the system claim only for hazard classes it can detect and intercept in time. Proposal frequency, conditional interception coverage, hardware faults, and common-cause failures need separate evidence. Oil or material failure outside the shield's sensing coverage stays in the residual-claims register.
:::

Operational fleet data may also violate the model behind the bound. Fleet-wide updates, shared layouts, and correlated weather can create common-cause events; the observation process and exposure model must account for them. A changed checkpoint cannot silently inherit older evidence, but an explicit configuration-equivalence argument may justify pooling relevant data. Human interventions should remain in the log as visited states and intercepted proposals, with authority flags and counterfactual adjudication where possible. A simulation contributes evidence only for the dynamics and disturbances it actually represents.

The shield calculation is a *conditional* architectural argument, not a multiplication applied to observed system incidents. For a defined hazard class $h$, let $\lambda_{\mathrm{proposal},h}$ be the rate of hazardous proposed actions before permission, and let $c_h=P(\mathrm{intercept}\mid\mathrm{hazardous\ proposal},h)$ be measured interception coverage for that class. With a separately bounded hardware and common-cause term $\lambda_{\mathrm{other}}$, a model may use @eq-frontier-shielded-hazard:
$$\lambda_{\mathrm{system},h} \le \lambda_{\mathrm{proposal},h}(1-c_h)+\lambda_{\mathrm{other}}$$ {#eq-frontier-shielded-hazard}
The relation requires a valid proposal oracle, timely detection, actuator authority, and a justified treatment of correlated failures. It gives no credit for an oil patch or brittle material state that the shield cannot observe. The illustrative 90-day proposal record and $c_h=0.9999$ in the notebook would still miss the $10^{-9}\text{ h}^{-1}$ target. No release follows from the arithmetic until each premise is supported.[^fn-hw-fault-registers]

[^fn-hw-fault-registers]: **Physical Trip Path**\index{Hardware fault register!trip}: Some configured comparator and gate-driver paths can remove commanded torque without waiting for the host scheduler. The pin response, drive behavior, mechanical stopping time, and clearance must be measured for the particular plant. Torque removal alone may permit coasting or gravity-driven motion.

::: {#chk-frontier-astronomical-exposure-wall-and-fleet-scaling .callout-checkpoint title="Exposure wall and distinct event rates"}

Before accepting fleet-scale statistical evidence for rare physical hazards, verify your understanding of exposure models, Poisson assumptions, and decomposed safety warrants:

- [ ] **Fleet evidence scope**: Which event does the zero-incident fleet record bound, and why can it not measure prevented hazardous proposals?
- [ ] **Statistical assumptions**: What stationary Poisson and fleet-dependence assumptions underlie $-\ln(0.05)/T$?
- [ ] **Decomposed warrants**: For a named hazard class, what separate proposal, interception, hardware, and common-cause evidence would justify @eq-frontier-shielded-hazard?
- [ ] **Exposure deficit**: Why does the illustrative 90-day proposal scenario with $c=0.9999$ still miss $10^{-9}\text{ h}^{-1}$?

:::

A planetary rover provides a different example. A long Earth–Mars communication delay rules out human correction of a fast drilling contact event. NASA/JPL describes software checks on force and torque, drill weight on bit, and tilt, with settings analyzed and tested for that operation. Those checks depend on their sensing, actuation, and geological assumptions; the cited account does not establish a passive torque clutch or guaranteed arrest before every rock failure ([NASA/JPL](https://science.nasa.gov/blog/ensuring-robotic-arm-safety-during-abrasions/)). @Fig-17-mars-perseverance-drill shows the arm and turret at the rock face where those onboard checks must hold. The photograph fixes the contact geometry and settles nothing about the response time behind it.

::: {#fig-17-mars-perseverance-drill fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Distant contact operation**: Perseverance's arm and turret work at a Martian rock outcrop. Communication delay makes the onboard force, torque, weight-on-bit, and tilt checks described by [NASA/JPL](https://science.nasa.gov/blog/ensuring-robotic-arm-safety-during-abrasions/) important to this operation; the photograph does not demonstrate a particular stop bound. Image: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS." fig-alt="Perseverance rover's robotic arm and drill turret near a Martian rock surface, with two nearby drilled holes visible. The image shows the contact setting, not the response time or guaranteed force of its protective checks."}
![](images/jpg/fig17_real_perseverance_mars_drill.jpg){width="85%" fig-alt="Perseverance rover's robotic arm and drill turret near a Martian rock surface, with two nearby drilled holes visible. The image shows the contact setting, not the response time or guaranteed force of its protective checks."}

## A Residual-Claims Register {#sec-frontier-residual-claims-register}

An unproven premise remains even if an engineer omits it from a safety report. When empirical testing cannot establish a safety bound, the unproven premise enters a formal **residual-claims register**\index{Residual-claims register!definition}. This auditable engineering ledger maps every unproven premise or unmonitored invariant to its missing physical observable, its active containment or operating restriction, an accountable human owner, and a predeclared closure test. An engineering team cannot treat an unverified physical assumption as an unwritten risk or temporary convenience. Without these four components, an unresolved claim is an open release claim.

Each entry links the unsupported claim to the specific unmeasurable physical observable. In an embodied system with physical authority over mass, a learned policy fails to settle a safety property because sensors cannot transduce the relevant environmental state, the computing substrate cannot process the measurement within the control deadline, or the physical interaction cannot be observed before contact occurs. An engineer must define the **missing observable**\index{Missing observable!definition} with physical precision rather than statistical abstractions. Characterizing an unknown failure as an "out-of-distribution latent state" provides no actionable signal for an enforcement loop to trigger a physical intervention. By contrast, stating an unmeasured surface friction coefficient, an undetected optical flare across a camera lens array, or an unobservable micro-fracture in an actuator housing identifies the exact physical deficit. Naming the missing observable establishes the boundary where learned inference stops and physical uncertainty begins.

In an analytical example, consider a $450\text{ kg}$ transport robot on depot concrete. Its proposed stopping claim assumes local tire–floor friction that a forward camera cannot establish beneath a clear oil film. With $v=0.9\text{ m/s}$ and the example's $17.1\text{ ms}$ response delay, $d=v\tau+v^2/(2\mu g)$ is about $0.36\text{ m}$ if $\mu\ge0.12$ is a validated floor. At $\mu=0.05$, braking alone is $0.826\text{ m}$ and the full stop is about $0.841\text{ m}$, exceeding the $0.50\text{ m}$ clearance. The proposed speed clamp is therefore conditional on measured or controlled floor conditions; it cannot establish safety on an unbounded oil slick. A lateral limit of $1.0\text{ m/s}^2$ also exceeds $\mu g$ at $\mu=0.05$.

An open entry requires an **operational response**\index{Operational response!definition}. For this depot, the operators can inspect and control the floor to support a friction lower bound, maintain physical separation barriers, and admit the $0.9\text{ m/s}$ restricted mode only within that validated envelope. If the lower bound cannot be supported, the release must exclude the route or withhold motion. The firmware limit reduces kinetic energy, but the response delay, achievable braking, and available clearance remain separate premises.[^fn-math-velocity-clamp]

[^fn-math-velocity-clamp]: **Velocity Kinetic Derating**\index{Velocity clamp!kinetic derating}: $E_k=mv^2/2$ decreases quadratically with speed. Stopping distance still depends on a validated braking floor and total response delay; a speed register alone cannot compensate for arbitrarily low friction.

The restricted mode needs an owner able to keep its physical premises true. The drivetrain lead controls the signed velocity and braking configuration; the depot operations manager maintains the inspected floor and separated walkways. Both record the inspection interval and the condition that withdraws permission. A claim about friction cannot be maintained by a firmware speed setting alone.

Every entry needs a **closure test**\index{Closure test!definition} declared before collecting data. For the depot, a candidate forward oil-film sensor must identify the specified contaminants early enough that the complete detection, permission, and braking path fits the measured clearance. A zero-miss result in 1,000 independent trials gives only a one-sided 95 percent miss-probability upper bound of $1-0.05^{1/1000}\approx0.002991$. Establishing a bound at or below $0.001$ under the same Bernoulli assumptions requires at least 2,995 independent, failure-free trials. The trial distribution, distance, latency, false alarms, and friction after detection must be declared. A wheel-slip reflex can limit later motion but cannot prove pre-contact friction. Only a validated end-to-end detector and stopping result could justify lifting the route restriction.

Specifying a closure test forces an engineering organization to determine whether a gap can be resolved with improved instrumentation and testing, or whether it represents a permanent unobservable state. When a closure test requires a physical transducer that is unavailable or cannot meet the response deadline, the register entry remains open. The operational restriction remains until the evidence changes. The danger arises when an organization treats an unclosable entry as a temporary backlog item, assuming that every physical failure mode can eventually be trapped by an onboard runtime detector.

The structured anatomy of these register entries is formalized across representative physical AI archetypes in @tbl-17-claims-register, illustrating how unmonitored hazards are systematically bounded by operational constraints until falsifiable closure tests are satisfied.

\Needspace{31\baselineskip}

| Claim and missing state                                                                         | Hazard mechanism                                                                                                                                        | Active containment and owner                                                                                                                                                                                   | Predeclared closure test                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Transport robot**: $d_{\rm stop}\le0.50\text{ m}$; local $\mu$ beneath clear oil is unknown.  | At $0.9\text{ m/s}$ and a $17.1\text{ ms}$ delay, the modeled stop is $\approx0.36\text{ m}$ at $\mu=0.12$ but $\approx0.841\text{ m}$ at $\mu=0.05$.   | Restrict speed only where inspection and floor controls support $\mu\ge0.12$; otherwise use barriers or withhold motion. *Owners*: drivetrain and depot operations leads.                                      | Characterize an independent forward contaminant sensor and full stop across a declared film distribution; at least 2,995 zero-miss independent trials for a 95% upper miss probability $\le0.001$, plus timing and clearance tests. |
| **Ceramic gripper**: brittle workpiece voids are not visible before contact.                    | With $k=500\text{ N/mm}$ and jaw speed $2\text{ mm/s}$, force rises $1000\text{ N/s}$ and reaches a $15\text{ N}$ fracture threshold at $15\text{ ms}$. | A calibrated $6\text{ N}$ preload, $2.5\text{ N/mm}$ compliant spring, and $3\text{ mm}$ hard stroke would limit the modeled force to $13.5\text{ N}$ if that force path is maintained. *Owner*: tooling lead. | Inspect internal voids with an independently validated method, or test the passive force path across the specified stroke, temperature, and wear envelope.                                                                          |

: **Residual-claims register matrix**: Auditable ledger of unproven physical premises across representative physical AI archetypes. For each open claim, the register defines the missing physical observable, the physical hazard mechanism, the active operational containment enforced by the nervous system or mechanical hardware, the accountable human owners, and the falsifiable closure test required to retire the operational restriction. {#tbl-17-claims-register tbl-colwidths="[22,24,26,28]"}

To ensure auditable tracking of unmonitored invariants across software deployments and physical revisions, safety-critical systems represent open residual claims through a formal, structured data contract (@tbl-17-residual-claims-schema). The abstract schema below defines the mandatory fields, scalar types, physical SI units, and structural invariants required for every unresolved physical assumption:
